### Our Greatly Gracious and Highly Honored Lord!

## Highly Honored Sir,

Although that part of <term>Natural Wisdom</term><note>A historical term for "Natural Philosophy," the study of the physical world and the precursor to modern science.</note> which deals with the transformation of metals is held in poor regard by almost everyone—even by many among the learned themselves who devote themselves to the investigation of nature and undertake to teach its secrets to others—this is partly because this art seems entirely incomprehensible to them and contrary to their <term>Aristotelian Philosophy</term><note>The traditional academic framework based on the teachings of Aristotle, which many alchemists felt was too theoretical and failed to account for experimental chemical changes.</note>. Furthermore, exceedingly few are found who can actually and in deed demonstrate those things of which those who have written of this wisdom speak and boast so much. It is also partly because daily many rogue <term>Sophists</term><note>In the context of alchemy, "sophists" or "puffers" were fraudulent practitioners who used trickery and false promises of gold-making to deceive wealthy patrons.</note> and impostors appear here and there under the name of "Philosophers," who through cunning malice and schemes, with great boasting, swearing, and assumed...

# Preface

Since the secret <term>philosophical vessel</term> <note>The specialized container, often a glass flask or "curcurbit," designed to withstand long periods of heat without allowing the "spirit" of the matter to escape.</note> along with the <term>philosophical fire</term> <note>Not merely common flame, but a carefully regulated, constant heat often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen.</note> are the two true master keys, without which the great <term>Stone of the Sages</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy, capable of perfecting base metals and human health.</note> cannot be composed and prepared, nor the sturdy lock of the royal chamber opened; and since the godly <term>Basil Valentine</term> <note>A legendary 15th-century Benedictine monk and alchemist; his works were highly influential in the 17th century.</note>, more than other philosophers, has most clearly and heartily described, designed, and depicted this same vessel;

Therefore, I have found it useful that this same vessel, standing on the table before Basil, be designed by a skilled master and placed before the eyes of every lover of this holy and laudable art. However, this vessel has been depicted and sketched in a <term>philosophical and veiled manner</term> <note>original: *verblümter Weise*. Alchemists intentionally used "flowery" or coded language and imagery to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note>, so that only those who are chosen for this high secret may reflect upon it with sharp insight and discover it alongside the philosophical fire; for these are gifts and presents from God, and must be prayed for and obtained from Him.

<term>Raymond Lully</term> <note>original: *Raymundus Lullius*. A 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many later alchemical texts were attributed.</note> writes of the vessel thus: "Yet we know of no other utensil or vessel but a single one, which we wish to clearly indicate here, in which vessel our work is carried out from the beginning to the end of the whole mastery."

**Basilius Valentinus** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, purportedly a Benedictine monk, though his writings appeared later.</note>, **Sendivogius** <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist known for his theory on the "food of life" in the air.</note>, and many other proven **philosophers** <note>original: *Philosophi*; at this time, "philosopher" often specifically referred to an alchemist or student of nature.</note> give the **sons of the art** <note>original: *Filiis artis*; a traditional term for initiated students of alchemy.</note> this teaching: that they should first study diligently with their minds and learn the art from books before they lay hands upon the work. For thus writes **Sendivogius** in the conclusion of his twelve small treatises:

> I have, dear reader, written these twelve small treatises for the benefit of the **children of the art**, so that before they grasp the work with their hands, they may learn to recognize the operations of **Nature**—specifically how she brings forth all things through her working—so that they do not try to enter the door without a key, or fetch water with a sieve. For he works in vain who attempts the labor in this holy and true art without knowledge of Nature; he is trapped in natural darkness, where the sun does not shine. He lies in thick shadow, where the moon does not shine at night.

We use these fires, and no more; the fire against nature must corrode the bodies <term>corpora: The physical substances or metals being worked upon.</term>. The **natural fire** is the third **solvent** <term>Menstruum: A solvent or "catalyst" used to dissolve solid materials; in Ripley’s system, the "third menstruum" is a highly refined substance.</term>; this fire lies hidden within every thing. The accidental fire we call the **Unnatural**, such as the ash-fire <note>A method of indirect heating where the glass vessel is placed in a bed of hot ashes.</note> and the fire of the **bath** <term>Balnei: Short for *Balneum Mariae* or Mary’s Bath, a water bath used for gentle, steady heating.</term> for the purpose of **rotting** <note>original: *putreficiren*; Putrefaction is the stage where the matter decomposes and turns black, a necessary step before it can be purified.</note>. Then your seed will rot and grow up with the help of the accidental fire, so that the same may afterwards be separated naturally.

Thus you must come through the **Gates of Separation**; then you can turn further toward the Gate of the **secret joining** <term>Conjunction</term>, which will lead you inside into the castle (take good note of this).

# Preface

Use my advice, if you wish to labor on the Work <note>The "Great Work" (*Magnum Opus*) refers to the arduous process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>; this gate is secured with two locks, as you will learn from what follows.

# Preface

...[at] ten o'clock set on fire, and in quick haste burned away everything I owned, so that I kept nothing in this world but my life, and might say with that philosopher: "All that is mine, I carry with me." <note>original Latin: *Omnia mea mecum porto*; a saying attributed to the Greek philosopher Bias of Priene, suggesting that true wealth lies in one's character and wisdom rather than physical possessions.</note>

In the fire, a **diamond ring** remained, which I had intended to give and honor my bride with. About five weeks after the fire, the golden ring was found again; however, the **diamond stone**, which had cost one hundred and forty-five **Reichsthaler** <term>Reichsthaler: A large silver coin used throughout the Holy Roman Empire; 145 thalers was a very significant sum, often exceeding the annual salary of a professional at the time.</term>, had sprung out because of the great heat and was judged to be lost. But finally, through the providence of **Almighty God**—who will not forsake those who fear Him, love Him, and rely upon Him—the little stone was found again in the first sieve when they began to wash the **dross** <term>dross: Original German *Krätze*, referring to the metallic waste, sweepings, or debris left over after a fire or smelting process.</term>. It had become more beautiful through the fire than it had been before; from this, I sensed that **God the Lord** wished to help me once more and to bless me.

To further describe the course of my life, I cannot leave the eager reader and seeker of the **art** <note>Refers to the "Hermetic Art" or alchemy.</note> uninformed that those who are to come to this high and great **secret** <note>The *Arcanum* or the mystery of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> are already foreseen and chosen by **GOD the LORD** from eternity, according to His great grace, love, and mercy, as the verses of **Johannis Ticinensis** <note>Johannes Ticinensis was a 14th-century Bohemian priest and alchemist whose rhythmic Latin verses were highly regarded by later seekers of the Stone.</note> state regarding this:

> The glowing **Stone** <note>original Latin: *Lapis candens*.</note> is made from three,
> To no one is it given, except to those
> To whom it comes by the **Breath of God** <note>original Latin: *DEI fit Spiramine*.</note>.

# Concerning the Great Stone of the Ancient Sages / by Brother Basilius Valentinus of the Benedictine Order.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'I' within a square woodcut frame featuring floral and scrolling foliage motifs.</image-desc>

I have, in my preface / dear friend and devotee of the Art <term>Art</term> <note>original: *Kunst*; in this context, it refers to the "Great Art" of alchemy, the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> / given promise / to you and others / who are eager / to learn the properties of Nature / and to research the arts from the heart / to show the cornerstone and rock / as much as has been permitted to me / and granted from above / from which our ancestors and the ancients / prepared their Stone / which they received from the Most High / to use for their health and the maintenance of this earthly life. So that I may now fulfill my promise and word / and not lead you astray into long-winded circuits through the errors of sophistry <term>sophistry</term> <note>original: *Sophisterey*; the author uses this to describe the deceptive or illogical practices of "false" alchemists who lacked true spiritual or chemical understanding.</note> / but rather reveal to you the main source of all goodness from its foundation.

Therefore you shall know / and take good heed of my following speech / if you otherwise desire to learn the Art / for I cannot provide much chatter / nor is it my intention / since the least is to be learned from it / but I love short words / that have a foundation within them.

Therefore, if you wish to work through our bodies <note>In alchemical philosophy, "bodies" (German: *Cörper*) refer to the physical metallic substances being transformed.</note>, then take the greedy **gray wolf**, who on account of his name is subject to the bellicose **Mars** <note>original: "Marti"; the gray wolf is a symbol for antimony, which was often associated with iron (Mars) in chemical processing because iron was used to reduce the antimony ore.</note>. By birth, however, he is a child of old **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturni"; Saturn is the planetary symbol for lead, suggesting the heavy, metallic origins of the substance.</note>, who is found in the valleys and mountains of the world, and is possessed by a great hunger. And when he has swallowed the King, then make a great fire and throw the wolf into it, so that he is consumed entirely; thus will the King be redeemed again. When this has happened three times, then the **Lion** has overcome the **Wolf**, and will find nothing more of him to consume; then our body is perfect for the beginning of our work.

And know that this alone is the right way, suitable for this purpose, to purify our bodies; for the **Lion** <note>original: "Leo"; the Lion often represents gold or the "fixed" principle that has been strengthened.</note> cleanses himself through the blood of the Wolf, and the blood's **tincture** <term>tincture|In alchemy, a tincture is a concentrated spiritual essence or medicinal "color" capable of permeating and transforming a substance.</term> rejoices marvelously with the tincture of the Lion, for the blood of both are in close kinship through their ancestry <note>original: "Gesipschafft"; this refers to the shared metallic nature of the materials.</note>. And when the Lion has been satiated, his spirit becomes stronger than before, and his eyes cast off a proud radiance, like the bright sun. His inner being is then capable of doing much, and is useful for all that is required of him; and when he is brought into his state of readiness, the children of men give thanks to him. Therefore, keep the following conclusion and meaning in mind regarding this discourse: a lowly thing cannot help another lowly thing, nor can it impart any advancement to its operation; and a combustible thing can provide no protection to another combustible thing to prevent it from burning. # The Ninth Key

The highest planet of the heavens, called **Saturn** <term>Saturn | in alchemy, this corresponds to the metal Lead; it represents the beginning of the work, associated with darkness, cold, and "base" matter</term>, has the least authority in our mastery, and yet he is the foremost **Key** of the entire Art. Through his **corruption** <note>original: *Verderbung*; here meaning the breaking down of the metal's form</note> he must come into improvement, so that **black is brought to white, and white into red**, passing also through the colors of the whole world’s course—which the other planets run through—until reaching the final **breeches-color** <note>original: *Hoſe-Farbe*; a traditional alchemical term for the deep reddish-purple or "kingly" color of the perfected Stone</note> of the triumphant King.

It then becomes such a malleable body as Saturn himself is, though subject to a much better constancy.

And although the person has drunk nothing but wine, from which the salt in his urine was made, it nonetheless has a different nature than the **Salt of Tartar** <term>Salt of Tartar</term> <note>original: "Weinstein"; a salt (potassium bitartrate) found in the sediment of wine barrels.</note>. This is because a **transmutation** <term>transmutation</term> has occurred within the human body, whereby the vegetable—that is, the **Spirit of Wine**—has become an **animal salt-spirit** <term>animal salt-spirit</term> <note>original: "animalischer Saltzgeist"; likely referring to ammonium salts derived from urea.</note>. This is similar to how horses cause a transformation of oats, hay, and the like into an increase of their strength, becoming fat in body and turning those things into flesh. Likewise, a bee makes honey from the noblest of flowers and herbs. This is to be understood of other things as well: the key and the cause lie solely in **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrifaction"; the process of decay or fermentation, which alchemists believed was necessary to release the "spirit" of a substance.</note> and decay, from which such separation and **transmutation** <term>transmutation</term> have their origin.

The **Common Spirit of Salt**, which is indeed driven out by the special method mentioned in my last report, makes **gold** and **silver** volatile if a small quantity of **Dragon-Spirit** <term>Dragon-Spirit</term> <note>original: "Drachen-Geiste"; often a metaphor for a strong corrosive acid, such as nitric acid or a specialized mercury derivative.</note> is added to it. It dissolves them and drives them high into the **beak of the helm** <note>The delivery tube or "nose" of the distillation head (alembic) through which vapors pass to be condensed.</note>, just as the **Eagle** <note>In alchemy, the "Eagle" often symbolizes the process of sublimation or the volatile principle itself.</note> does with the dragon-spirit that creeps in and out of the rocky cliffs. However, if something is melted with **salt** before its spirit is separated from its body, it **fixes** the substance much more than it makes it volatile.

## On Common Sulfur.

Commonly used sulfur is not yet exalted to such a perfect degree, nor brought to such ripeness, as it is found in antimony <term>Spießglaß<gloss>stibnite or antimony ore, which alchemists believed contained a more "mature" or "pure" sulfur than the common yellow variety</gloss></term> and vitriol. Now, an oil is made from it by itself <note>original: "per se"</note> for foul, stinking wounds; it also kills the worms that grow therein, especially if the salt of sulfur (the quantity of which is very small) has been dissolved in it.

A balsam is also made from it with tree or juniper oil, as well as with the white spirit of turpentine. It is red in color, and this occurs when the flowers of sulfur <term>flores des Schwefels<gloss>the fine powder produced when sulfur is sublimated by heat</gloss></term> are prepared through a *colcothar* of vitriol <term>Colchotar des Vitrioli<gloss>the red iron oxide residue remaining after the distillation of vitriol; used here as a catalyst or medium</gloss></term> and digested for a time in horse dung <note>A common alchemical method for providing a gentle, consistent heat over several weeks</note> or otherwise. This same balsam is good to use internally for those suffering from lung disease <note>original: "Lungensüchtigen"; likely referring to consumption or tuberculosis</note>, especially if it is first rectified several times with the spirit of wine <note>distilled alcohol</note>, drawn over, and separated until it has become blood-red; for this balsam preserves against decay.

If a person is possessed by blindness, they cannot pass judgment on any writing; but understanding judges with patience, and wisdom separates itself from folly through its own experience.

# ON THE MICROCOSM <note>original Latin: "De Microcosmo"</note>

Thus, one nature follows after another, unfathomable and incomprehensible. For the time being, it remains unknown to the common man—who is not concerned with learning the ways of nature—and is even regarded by him as quite unbelievable.

But to speak again of man: the noblest spirit of life has its dominion and dwelling most strongly in the heart of the human body, as the most noble place. The <term>Sulfur of man; original Latin: "Sulphur hominis"; the oily, soul-like principle of heat and growth</term> provides such a spirit with nourishment and a spiritual pathway for its preservation through the air. For when air is taken away from a person, the spirit of life must suffocate and departs invisibly, and thus the death of the human has already appeared. 

The noblest <term>Salt-spirit; original: "Salȝ-Geift"; the alchemical principle of stability and preservation</term>, however, is a preserver of both <note>referring to the sulfur and the spirit of life</note>. Its noblest spirit permeates everything, but the coarsest matter of its salt is cast off into the bladder. This substance, however, possesses a <term>spirit; original Latin: "Spiritum"</term> of a particular kind and operation. And whatever of the salt passes out through the bladder, heat acts upon it again and provides a new gateway, so that the supply of salt in man is inexhaustible until he passes away entirely, his body is burnt to ash, and the remaining <term>residue; original Latin: "residuum"</term> is extracted. 

Take a similar example from all the <term>salts of minerals; original: "Salȝ der Mineralien"</term>, which grow again through heat, <term>coagulate; thicken or solidify</term>, and allow themselves to be extracted through <term>wateriness; original: "Wäfserigkeit"</term>. In particular, all common salts and <term>saltpeter; a mineral salt (potassium nitrate) used in alchemy and gunpowder</term> earth provide certainty of this, and thus further examples are judged unnecessary at this time.

The fire in the heart and the natural warmth are maintained by the air, which must reside within it. The lungs have the greatest need for the help of this air. Another medicine is prepared from antimony, regarding which I have found that it has accomplished excellent and high things in fevers that have arisen, of whatever kind they may be, as well as in the time of the <term>plague</term> <note>original: *Pestilenz*</note>; namely, that the **antimony** is ground very small, then put into a glass, and thus driven over strongly with fire in a **retort** <note>original: *Retorten*; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling or sublimating substances.</note> without any addition, for the third or fourth time, into a large receiver glass; in the end, a red powder results from it. Extract this with **vinegar** <note>original: *aceto*</note>; let this **extraction** circulate with a gentle fire for ten days long; then **distill** the vinegar away from it, and what remains must be completely driven over into an **oil** <note>original: *oleum*</note> by a special manual technique. This oil is further circulated and **pelicanized** <note>original: *pellicanirt*; a process of continuous distillation where the condensed liquid flows back into the main body of the flask, named after the "pelican" vessel which resembles the bird pecking its own breast.</note> until the moisture has left it and it has once again become a powder—after the vinegar was initially separated from it through **distillation** and the final **oil** was caught in a new receiver.

Taking four grains of this oil with a **distilled water of Blessed Thistle** <note>original: *Cardebenedicten*; a plant historically used in monastic medicine to treat fevers and infections.</note> and being warmly covered thereafter, and sweating well upon it, cures the second, third, and fourth-day **fevers** <note>The author refers here to "tertian" and "quartan" fevers, which were characterized by the intervals of days between paroxysms.</note>. Used in the same weight with a **spirit of wine** <note>original: *Spiritu vini*; high-proof alcohol.</note> or a distilled wine vinegar—depending on whether the plague initially showed itself with chills or heat—it has been found to have remarkable virtue in driving the same away. This was seen in our monastery when three of my fellow brothers, who at the same time were nearly surrendered to death by such a plague and had entirely [concluded] their last wills...

<gloss><unclear>A little piece of Antimony</unclear></gloss>
This metallic lump <term>Regulus</term> <note>The metallic mass found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting.</note> or Star of Signature, also called salt armoniac <note>original: *sal armo*; likely referring to ammonium chloride used as a flux</note>, is frequently brought through the fire with the Stone-Serpents <note>original: *SteinSchlangen*; an alchemical metaphor for the corrosive or transformative minerals added to the antimony</note>, so that it is finally entirely consumed therein, and joins and incorporates itself completely with the Serpents. When this has happened, the seeker of the Art has a material <note>original: *Materia*</note> that is entirely fiery and hot; much of the Art lies buried in this. This prepared material also dissolves into an Oil; this same Oil must then be driven over through distillation and afterwards purified <note>original: *rectificirt*</note> so that it becomes pure with the spirit <note>original: *met spiritu*</note> and becomes entirely clear.

This Oil can also be safely and quite well used internally in the body, yet with great caution and moderation; not more than twice a week, and no more than three drops at once in two ounces of wine, or another suitable distilled herbal water, according to the purpose for which it is to be used.

Therefore, every physician should take heed and first recognize the cause of the illness, alongside observing the temperament <term>Complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of "humors" (fluids like blood and bile) believed to determine a person's health and personality.</note> of the patient, so that he can use his remedies all the more safely accordingly.

This is of a very great potency, and many wonders lie hidden behind it, which are not necessary to reveal all at once to the unlearned; rather, some arts must also remain behind, so that secrets <note>original: *Arcana*</note> and mysteries <note>original: *Mysteria*</note> remain for the philosopher <note>original: *Philosopho*</note>, who has often and daily applied much bitter labor to fathom such secrets. But whoever wishes to follow in my footsteps, let him not be vexed by the trouble of searching, but do as I have done, so he will also attain that...

# Triumphal Chariot

Love surpasses all other infirmities and diseases, for it can in no way be helped except through a remedy of its own kind <note>The author alludes to the homeopathic principle of "like cures like," suggesting that the "disease" of love can only be cured by the object of that love.</note>, which is the desire of both natures. This is only extinguished through the fulfillment of the will of that ignited and captured longing. Even in this current hour, many must testify to what love can do; for it does not only look upon the young, but also the old, who burn entirely, rave, and rage so much in their old age because of love that they become complete fools on its account.

Other natural diseases also regulate themselves according to the **complexion** <term>Complexion: In early modern medicine, this refers to an individual's "temperament" or the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within their body</term> of the person, affecting one individual more violently than another. Love, however, makes no distinction whatsoever; rather, when it arrives, it strikes equally through rich and poor, old and young people alike, and fears no snare, no matter how wicked it may be.

<margin><unclear>S. M. P.</unclear></margin>
In other natural weaknesses and ailments, a person feels only certain limbs that suffer pain and have been overtaken by it, while the remaining limbs meanwhile enjoy rest and peace. But love infects and takes over the entire body, with its entire **substance** <term>Substance: The essential physical reality of the body, as opposed to its mere outward appearance</term>, being, and form—nothing is excluded in the slightest. For the heart is so filled with **ardor** <term>Ardor: (German: *Brunst*) a state of intense heat or passionate burning, often used in alchemical texts to describe the "hunger" one substance has for another</term> that a distribution follows into all the veins and limbs of the entire body. # The Triumphal Chariot

...martyrdom, which will endure forever without end or ceasing; may [He] graciously protect [us from this].

Everyone should know, however, that our stone, called *Fire* <note>original: "Ignis"</note>, must be boiled and brought to maturity by physical fire within the Little World <note>The "Microcosmus" or Little World refers to the human sphere and the alchemist's laboratory, which mirrors the "Macrocosmus" or the universe at large.</note>, just as other foods and medicines must be prepared. For where the fire of the Great World finishes its work, the Little World begins to bring about a new birth; therefore, no person should truly wonder at this process of boiling.

Wheat is increased and ripened by the elemental fire of the Great World <note>The natural heat of the sun and the seasons.</note>; however, it is only through the physical fire of the Little World <note>Human arts, such as cooking or baking.</note> that another new boiling and ripening is accomplished, so that humans can further use that blessing for their own sustenance. In this way, the last and smallest thing—which was produced from the great and first thing—can fulfill its purpose.

The true *Oil of Antimony* <note>original: "oleum Antimonii"; a potent chemical extract believed to have profound medicinal and alchemical properties.</note>, from which the stone called *Fire* is prepared, possesses an exceedingly great and sweet quality. It is separated and purified from its earth <note>original: "terra"; the solid residue or dross remaining after distillation or extraction.</note> in such a way that if a small vial of it is placed in the sun, it casts out many diverse and wonderful rays. It is as if countless fiery mirrors were present in a room or chamber, gleaming ruby-red and with many other marvelous colors.

Now listen, my dear seeker of the Art, you who love the truth and intend to learn something, and are eager to discover more:

Take, in the name of the Most High, Antimony <note>original: "Spießglaß"; the historical name for the mineral stibnite, the primary ore of antimony.</note>.

# of Antimony. 451

<margin><unclear>scribble</unclear> 342</margin>
Take one part ore that has grown toward the sunrise <note>Alchemical symbolism suggesting ore from the east or ore of a specific ripeness.</note>, and one part Saltpeter <note>Potassium nitrate, a powerful oxidizing agent in early chemistry.</note> that is good and pure; grind it all small and mix it together; then place it in a moderate fire; burn or calcine <note>original: "glües"; to heat a substance to a high temperature without melting it to change its chemical properties.</note> it together according to the manual technique which is the masterpiece; then a substance remains which is inclined toward a brown color. Turn that substance into a glass <note>A vitrified or translucent material produced by high heat.</note>; grind that same glass small again, and extract the deep red **tincture** <note>original: "Tinctur"; a concentrated extract or essence.</note> from it with a pure, good, and sharp distilled vinegar made from its own mineral. Draw off the vinegar through **distillation** in a **water bath** <note>original: "Balneo Mariæ"; a double-boiler method providing gentle, indirect heat.</note>, so that a powder remains behind. Extract that powder once more with **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spiritu vini"; concentrated alcohol or ethanol.</note> brought to its highest purity; then the dregs <note>original: "feces"; the solid residue or sediment.</note> remain behind, and you have an exceedingly beautiful red **extraction**, sweet and lovely, which is highly useful to use in medicine.

<margin>454</margin>
That is now the pure **Sulfur of Antimony** <note>original: "Sulphur Antimonii"; in alchemy, 'sulfur' represents the active, soulful, or flammable principle of a substance.</note>, separated to the highest degree. If you have 2 pounds of this extraction, then take eight *Lot* <note>A historical unit of weight, approximately 1/32nd of a pound or 15 grams.</note> of **Salt of Antimony** <note>original: "Salis Antimonii"; the 'body' or crystalline essence of the substance.</note>, as I have taught you to make; pour this extraction onto it and circulate <note>A process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel, often called refluxing today.</note> it well together for at least one month, well sealed, so the salt will have united itself with the extraction of sulfur. If it has deposited dregs, then separate them from it, and first distill the **spirit of wine** from it in the **bath of the Holy Virgin Mary** <note>A pious name for the water bath or *Balneum Mariae*.</note>. The powder that remains for the artist, drive with a strong fire; then, with great and unbelievable wonder, many colors pass over, and a lovely sweet **oil** <note>original: "oleum"</note> comes across, completely transparent and red in its dissolution. Rectify <note>To purify a liquid by repeated distillation.</note> this oil once more in a **water bath** until the fourth part of it comes over; then it is <margin><unclear>regent</unclear></margin> right.

<margin>409</margin> When that has also been done and accomplished, take the **living Mercury of Antimony** <note>original: "lebendigen Mercurium des Spießglase"; a refined essence of the mineral antimony, which alchemists believed was its "inner soul" or metallic spirit.</note> as I have also taught you to make; and pour upon it a red **oil of vitriol** <note>original: "oleum vitrioli"; concentrated sulfuric acid.</note> made from iron <note>original: "auß Eisen gemacht"; referring to "oil of Mars," or sulfuric acid derived from iron sulfate.</note> and rectified <note>original: "rectificirt"; purified by repeated distillation.</note> to the highest degree. To this end, the **spirit** of the oil assists mightily, which remains behind with the Mercury and unites with it.

Take one part of this **precipitate** and one part of the previous **oil** <note>The "Sulfur of Antimony" or the oil described on page 451.</note> made sweet from the Antimony; pour them together and place them in a small **phial** <note>original: "Phiolein"; a glass bottle.</note>, well-sealed. In time, the precipitate will dissolve into the oil through a steady, constant heat and will **fix** <note>original: "figiren"; the alchemical process of turning a volatile substance into a stable one that can endure fire.</note>. Furthermore, the phlegm will be consumed by the fire, and ultimately it will become a red, dry, fixed, and **fusible powder** <note>original: "flüssigem Pulver"; a powder that remains solid but melts like wax when heated, without evaporating.</note>, which will show no sign of smoke.

My dear disciple, apostle, or artist of the mystery: I will now speak in the manner and fashion of the Prophets, and I say thus: When you have brought your **studies of philosophy** <note>original: "Studia der Philosophiæ"; here meaning the study of alchemy and the secrets of nature.</note> this far toward their end, alongside the completed work of Antimony as I have now and hereby prescribed to you, then you possess a **medicine** for both humans and metals. ## Preface and Introduction

# BROTHER BASIL VALENTINE,

->Of the Benedictine Order.<-

Since the time is at hand that I, by the will of God my Creator and His dear Son Jesus Christ, must close my laboratory <note>Basil Valentine uses the "laboratory" as both a physical space for alchemical work and a spiritual metaphor for the human life where the soul is refined.</note> here in this transitory world, and proceed from day to day—indeed, from hour to hour—to appeal from that same earthly laboratory to the true heavenly one; and since the end is near to conclude my life through the appointed goal of the supreme throne of grace <note>original: "Gnadenthron"; a biblical reference to the mercy seat or the presence of God where one receives grace.</note> of Jesus Christ; and as I daily sigh and carry a heartfelt longing for the true bread of heaven <note>original: "Himmelbrod"; referring to spiritual nourishment and eternal life.</note> of eternal salvation, where riches and everlasting joy are in abundance and without end: it has also seemed fitting to me, and I have felt and considered it in my conscience as highly necessary, to establish a Christian reconciliation with my fellow Christians, those now living in this world and those to come after me. I do this so that my soul, in the peace and patience of the summons of my dear God, may await the Heavenly Paradise and dwelling, and remain in readiness day and night to be inscribed in the Book of Life. By which

<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: He.</meta>

<summary>In this solemn preface, the author, writing as the monk Basil Valentine, prepares for his death by framing his alchemical life as a spiritual "laboratory" and seeking reconciliation with his readers.</summary>
<keywords>Basil Valentine, Benedictine, laboratory, salvation, throne of grace, bread of heaven, reconciliation, Book of Life, alchemy, deathbed testament</keywords>

</margin>

In this consideration, I simultaneously recall all my writings which I have previously recorded and published—just as the Ancients did before me. I wish to reveal and leave behind all the secrets of Nature for the benefit of the artists, the eager disciples seeking the Art, and the diligent researchers of these mysteries—at least as much as has been revealed and granted to me by the highest **Spagyrist** <note>original: "Spagyro"; a term coined by Paracelsus referring to an alchemist who separates and recombines substances to create medicine.</note> and heavenly **Physician** <note>original: "Medico"; here referring to God as the source of all healing knowledge.</note>, and as much as I have been permitted to bequeath.

Thus, I have further resolved—not without a great urging of my conscience and for the advancement of Christian love—to fulfill my promise and pledge by providing a more extensive and necessary account of Nature and the essential, knowledgeable techniques <note>original: "Handgriff"; literally "hand-grips," referring to the practical, manual operations of laboratory alchemy.</note> of the artist. I intend to describe these from the foundation of truth, to uncover them, and to make them known through understandable speech: namely, in what manner and way the closed, bolted, and manifold locks of Nature may be slid back, the door to all the world's treasures opened, and the knowledge of all secrets above all secrets be grasped—which are to be attained through the sharpening of the intellect and the persistence of beloved prayer.

Although neither compulsion nor pressure has been placed upon me—and much less have I been incited by my own fame or vanity to write down and leave behind even a single letter—I have nevertheless considered the misery and wretchedness of this world, in which the children of obscurity and darkness have fallen; indeed, they are almost completely perishing.

He frames the discovery of nature's secrets as a process requiring both practical laboratory skill and devout prayer.</summary>
<keywords>alchemical secrets, Spagyrist, Christian love, laboratory techniques, nature's locks, spiritual darkness, Basil Valentine</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface of Brother Basil Valentine. Having previously stated his intent to leave behind his knowledge for the benefit of others, Valentine now laments the decline of true medical knowledge and the rise of academic physicians who lack practical experience.</meta>

### Brother Basil Valentine.

Oh God, how my spirit is troubled when I consider the folly of this contemptible world and the blindness of all its children—who nevertheless consider themselves noble and wise, having attended **universities** <note>original: "hohen Schulen"; literally "high schools," referring to the scholastic institutions of the time, which Valentine frequently criticized for favoring book-learning over practical experience.</note>, and imagining they have gathered great understanding within their minds. Where has the high and precious medicine of the ancient, wise masters flown—those who lived before any university was even built or invented? They received their revelation solely through heartfelt, pleading prayer to God and through daily investigation and **manual labor** <note>original: "HandArbeit"; a technical term in alchemy referring to the practical, physical operations performed in a laboratory, such as distillation and calcination.</note>. Where, I ask, has their toil and labor vanished? Nowhere else than in the old, cavernous, unclean, and moldy apothecary shops, plunged deep into the earth and buried—indeed, completely sunken, such that they cannot be awakened again by any **sound of the mortar** <note>original: "Mörsel-klang"; the rhythmic sound of a pestle in a mortar, the traditional symbol of the pharmacist's craft.</note> to further spread and demonstrate their praise with wonder and with the glorification of the Most High.

But I know for certain that when my writings properly come to light and appear before the day after my death, and are rightly read, contemplated, and understood by wise descendants, apostles, and disciples of wisdom—and are furthermore sought and worked upon with a Christian purpose, for no other reason than the glory of God and the love of one’s fellow Christian—that through such right and well-founded labor, all the bumbling and bungling of those supposed, boastful, vainglorious fellows and high-flown fools will be [exposed]. These are the ones who describe themselves and present themselves as physicians and masters of **both medicines** <note>original: "beyder Artzneyen"; likely referring to the Paracelsian concept of medicine for both the internal body and external wounds, or the medicine of both the body and the spirit.</note>—that is, writing of things internal and external—and who desire to be held in high honor for it...

# Preface.

[the] day will come and be revealed, upon which alone all their foundation and purpose is built and directed—namely, to possess great honor, to acquire fame with a guilty conscience, to obtain money through the deception of one's neighbor, to live in high esteem and reputation, and to strive for <term>dignities</term> <note>original: "Dignitäten"; referring to high offices, academic titles, or positions of social status within the hierarchy of the time.</note>. They are filled to the ears with devilish splendor, pride, and vanity; and finally, with misery, woe, and the lamentation of their poor souls, they shall be wretchedly submerged. Oh, woe upon woe unto you, children of the Devil! Indeed, it is not my intention in this place to use such long-windedness, nor to introduce such matters that do not serve my purpose; rather, this shall be saved for the end of this book, as a blessed <term>farewell</term> <note>original: "Valete"; a Latin valediction or parting word used at the conclusion of a work.</note> and the closing of all my writings. There—provided the Prince of Heaven preserves my life for long and grants that I may write further—as a final appendix to all my works, everyone shall be further warned by me and diligently urged to seek the true <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "Medicin"; in the alchemical tradition, this refers not just to a cure for illness, but to the "Universal Medicine" or Tincture that heals both the human body and "sick" (imperfect) metals.</note> with which one desires to meet, assist, and serve one's neighbor, seeking it in those things wherein it was ordained and placed by God the Creator to be found, etc.

This present book of mine may justly be called the Glimmer and Light of all Darkness; for everything that I outlined in my previous writings by way of parables / and wrote and indicated as befits a <term>philosopher</term> <note>original: "Philosopho"; here meaning a "philosopher of the fire" or alchemist, who traditionally hid secrets behind metaphors and allegories.</note>, that shall be explained in this my final report, demonstrated and proven with clear, bright words. The <term>matter</term> <note>original: "Materia"; the "Materia Prima" or starting substance required for the alchemical Great Work.</note> shall be publicly named, and the manual operations of all preparations from the beginning [shall be shown].

->### Brother Basilius Valentinus.<-

...means and end indicated and described in the clearest way; all and every <term>matter</term> <note>original: "Materia"; in alchemy, this refers to the physical substances or "prime matter" required for the Great Work.</note> presented and set before one's eyes; the truth confirmed; and the <term>foundation</term> <note>original: "Grund"</note> distinguished from the <term>unground</term> <note>original: "Ohngrund"; a mystical term referring to the "groundless" or "bottomless" nature of the divine before creation, or the void from which all things emerge.</note> in such a way that even children can understand it and grasp it with their hands.

However, because this book grants and bestows a much different kind of <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "Wissenschafft"; here meaning a sacred or hidden science rather than modern academic science.</note> than my other writings—in which I did not write quite so obscurely, nor did I use such subtlety as the <term>ancients</term> <note>original: "die Alten"; referring to the previous generations of alchemists and philosophers who often wrote in riddles.</note> (who concluded their lives before me) have done—this book will also require a much different place for safekeeping, where it might be kept hidden from the evil, base world. 

Although it shall not be buried with me and become the portion of worms, but shall be preserved and left upon the earth; yet, remaining unknown to the evil world, it shall be kept safely in a special secret place through the grant of the Creator, where no one shall come except he to whom it is granted by God. Whereas, on the other hand, my other writings will come to light much more promptly and sooner.

You should also know, whoever you may be, who shall come to and attain this my Last Testament and revelation of the heavenly and earthly secrets—you who find it—that such a thing will happen in no other way than through the will and special <term>providence</term> <note>original: "Versehung"; the protective care and preparation of God.</note> and calling of the Holy Heavenly Trinity. Into whose keeping, alongside the invocation previously made, I have commended it, deposited and laid it here, together with that which accompanies it; for it was not without cause that I left it behind for whomever it may be gran-

->### Preface.<-

...be seen, granted, and bestowed. For it is in no way fitting to allow **God’s** creation and mystery—which are already far too hidden, and which have stepped from the light into darkness because of the roguery and malice of the sinful world—to perish entirely, as the envious and hateful-hearted are inclined. Rather, for the sake of conscience, I wish to leave behind a glimpse of the truth and of the bright heavens, and to lay down again that talent <note>original: "Pfund"; a reference to the biblical Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25, implying a God-given gift or responsibility that must be put to use for the master's benefit.</note> which was granted and revealed to me entirely without merit by the Almighty, and to deliver it back into His faithful hand, and to commend it to His protection and diligent care, preservation, and industry; to Him may it be herewith commended unto all eternity.

For I, as a monk <note>original: "Clostermann"; literally "cloister-man."</note> and unworthy servant of the Divine, infinite Trinity, acknowledge and say: that in the <term>science</term> <note>original: "Wissenschafft"; here referring to a sacred or specialized knowledge of natural laws.</note> of those infinite mysteries—the dissection of <term>natures</term> <note>original: "Naturen"; in this context, the inner essences or spiritual properties of physical substances</note>, the improvement and alteration of their qualities for the abundant sustenance of this life, and the knowledge of the true <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "Artzney"</note> ordained by God—with which I have assisted my fellow men, all and every one who desired it of me, until this time, and which I shall not cease to do further until my final end—I would never have reached or come so far, had not many books—written and left behind by the old masters who passed away long before me—been bestowed upon me through **God’s** special goodness, grace, and mercy. These [books] were granted to me with no little joy and heartfelt thanksgiving to God, in this my monastery, in a wondrous way...

# Brother Basilius Valentinus.

...seen, and most of all came into my hands through the Providence of God. Without seeking any personal glory, I have shown as much good to my fellow Christians as was humanly possible for me; for which they, but above all God, have thanked me even unto the grave.

Now, however, since I can no longer be a steward <note>original: "Haußhalter"; a biblical reference to the role of a household manager or caretaker of a master's property.</note>, having done my part, let another not allow his own diligence to falter. Therefore, I commend such faithful stewardship of mine back into the faithful hand of God, into His omnipotence and faithful keeping. I deliver back into His administration—to His divine glory, power, and majesty—instead of the keys to the household, all His mysteries <term>mysteria</term> <note>refers to the secret alchemical and spiritual knowledge granted by God</note> written down here, to bestow them further after my death upon whomever His divine will has chosen and selected. May it be applied and granted for the best: with the acknowledgment of His praiseworthy name, heartfelt thanksgiving, and the service and benefit of one's neighbor, while avoiding worldly splendor, pride, arrogance, luxury, presumption, greed, lusts, and contempt.

O Lord, Almighty God, merciful and kind Father of your dear, only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, you who alone are the Lord of Hosts <note>original: "Zebaoth"; a Hebrew title for God (Sabaoth) meaning "Lord of Armies," emphasizing His power over all creation.</note>, the beginning of all things which were made through your Word, and before whom all heavenly and hellish creatures must tremble and quake: I, a poor miserable man, sinner, and earth-worm, thank you with my stammering tongue from the innermost center <term>Centro</term> <note>the "center" or heart, often used in alchemy to refer to the essential core of a substance or the soul.</note> of my heart, that you have made known to me the great light of the heavenly and earthly...

## On the Exit and Entry of Metals.

<margin>16.</margin>
The work of metals testifies to a constant exiting and entering of the metals; for by "exit" one should understand not only the departure of the entire work—whereby a mine in one place completely perishes when it has nothing left to consume and has exhausted <unclear>all</unclear> of its own bodies <note>original: *corpora*</note>—but also the partial exit. For one [part] always seeks the other and follows closely on its heels. You can see this clearly in metallic mercury <note>original: *Mercurio metallo*</note> when you pour it out: how it divides itself into many hundreds of small, lively grains, which nevertheless all flow back together into one body <note>original: *corpus*</note>. The volatile and the slippery <note>original: *volatile uñ lubricum*</note> behave in this same way. But the <term>Ferch</term> <note>An archaic mining term referring to the "vital sap" or life-force of the ore, believed to give the rock its metallic value</note> also exits piece by piece in this manner, until it finally comes together in one place. And just as bees meet one another, so the <term>Ferch</term> does from one piece to another, until it comes together again in a certain place, as much of it as is necessary; for it tolerates no more than it requires. The rest and the remainder thus swarms out and into another workshop <note>Refers to a different geological vein or cavity where ore forms</note>. Such division then results in many and various kinds of mines, depending on how the workshop and the nourishment <note>original: *Speise*, referring to the mineral-rich fluids that "feed" the growth of metals</note> are prepared, and according to how one also encounters it in his work, during the exit.

->or<-

Since, however, through the work of mining one makes an intrusion into nature, one also obtains many kinds of metal; therefore, one must make a distinction between them, so that one might not suffer loss or waste in the labor. For knowing how to distinguish the metal by its colors is indeed a fine knowledge—such as red-gold ore <note>original: *Rohtgülden*; a silver ore now known as pyrargyrite</note>, vitreous ore <note>original: *Glaß-Ertz*; silver glance or acanthite</note>, green, or black ore, etc. Yet, nonetheless, one does not yet know its [manner of] processing quite thoroughly. ## CHAPTER 10.
# OF PURE METAL, <note>original: *DE METALLO PURO*</note>
->or<-
# Of the fine Metal.

When the metal—be it in the ascending or descending <note>Refers to the alchemical cycles of refinement, where "ascending" relates to sublimation or vaporization and "descending" to precipitation or solidification</note>—is in its seven systems <note>original: *Systematibus*; likely referring to the seven stages of transformation or the seven planetary metals</note> or states, it rests and purifies itself until it finally enters into another body <note>original: *corpus*</note>. If one then encounters such an ore, that is the very purest metal that one can find and have in the world; here among our smelters, we call such a thing "super-fine." But our "super-fine," as it has been used until now, is an impure thing compared to this; for if it lacks even a small grain <term>grain: a traditional, tiny unit of weight used by jewelers and assayers to measure purity</term> in the refining process, it is not yet correct. Such metal is now, as one might imagine, very good and malleable, and nothing is lost during any of the work; and although one can "super-fine" all metals <note>original: *metalla*</note>, one can make none purer than Gold <note>represented by the symbol ☉</note>; for thereafter, no element attacks the gold anymore such that it could take anything from it, make a spoil <note>original: *spolio*; a loss of material or "loot" taken by the fire</note> of it, or nullify it.

The silver at Markirch <note>modern Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines</note> in Lorraine is thus super-fine and pure of all other metals; for "super-fining" actually means when a metal is pure of all other metals; for the fact that it is otherwise impure from dross <note>original: *excremento*; the waste or byproduct of the smelting process</note> can easily be remedied and does not harm its fineness. Thus, in all silver mines, one often finds such a natural specimen <note>original: *Prob*</note> of a pure and fine ore that one could almost mint it immediately; and although one must melt—

For an awake and a sleeping body accomplish nothing; they must both be awake. Thirdly, you must pay close attention to the **flow** <note>original: *Fluß*; both the state of being molten and the "flux" added to help the metal melt</note>, so that you liberate it as you would a raw substance that is itself still liquid; for if one opens both flows completely, it is then difficult to bring them back together again. ### The 1st Book, 15th Chapter

The ore or metal then takes in the **inhalation** <note>original: *Einwitterung*; the process by which the earth "breathes in" celestial or atmospheric influences.</note> that arises from its internal work, and makes use of it; for one sees that the physical elements cannot penetrate deep into the earth. When a metal "works" <note>Refers to the natural alchemical process of maturation within the rock.</note>, it gives off this breath from itself and also draws it back to itself. The outward breath is the "weathering" that follows; the inward breath, however, is this: for with it, the earth must split open and pull the influence into itself so that it may form a <term>body</term> <note>original: *corpus*; the physical substance of the metal.</note>. To this end, the sun must provide assistance, for where the <term>system</term> <note>original: *Systema*; here meaning the organized structure or constitutional arrangement of the mineral.</note> accompanies the weathering—which must be recognized with great skill—there is the purest earth. According to the testimony of some of the Ancients, it is from this pure earth that humanity was first taken; and such earth possesses much hidden power within it for the subsequent refinement of metals. 

Such "inhalation" serves only this purpose, as you have just heard: that it draws in, swallows, and soaks the "food" <note>The nourishing celestial influence or "astral seed."</note> into the <term>body</term>. For you must not think that it simply leaves it lying in the <term>body</term> once it has been brought inside; rather, it is the <term>retentive force</term> <note>original: *vis retentiva*; the power of a substance to hold onto its vital nutrients or qualities.</note> by which it keeps that which has been soaked up and fed into it steady and firm. 

For this purpose, it prepares the material throughout the entire journey from the place where it receives it from the sun, which then drives everything that is heavy downward. This can be seen in all **sap** <note>original: *Safft*; the vital liquid essence or "mercury" of the metals.</note> that is driven downward in this manner. In this downward pull, however, it has this quality: the longer and deeper the saps descend, the better and more highly the earth brings them into their <term>blossoms</term> <note>original: *flores*; the refined, essential chemical states or "flowers" of a mineral.</note>.

# The First Book, Chapter 18.

...the weathering <term>weathering</term> <note>original: *Witterung*; in early mining and alchemy, this referred to the movement of vapors, air, and mineral "scents" through the earth which were thought to nourish or refine ores.</note> can go no further, because the metal is the end-point of the work under the earth; therefore, the exhalation must find its way there and turn back within that same metal. From this, it cleanses whatever is to be cleansed in the work—and not only in the work or the workshop <note>The "workshop" refers to the specific vein or pocket where a mineral grows.</note>, but in the entire apparatus, until it even lifts and expels the pure **atoms** <term>atoms</term> <note>original: *atomos*; here meaning the smallest, most refined particles of matter rather than the modern physical atom.</note> of the earth. Nature cannot tolerate them, nor are they of any use in the earth; instead, they must be **resolved** again in the upper air. 

This exhalation, however, though it is always present with the metal, can be seen by its **rods** <term>rods</term> <note>original: *Ruthen*; this may refer to the "streaks" or branches of a mineral vein, or the dowsing rods used by miners to sense the "weathering" of the ore.</note> what the ore is doing. For if this same weathering attacks the rods and ignites them, then the metal is in its decline and is a **dead metal** <note>A metal that has lost its vital growth force, often resulting in base or brittle material.</note>. It carries out more fire, which ignites this rod; conversely, cold remains with the lower metal and gains the upper hand. Thus, one sees what the **burning blights** <term>burning blights</term> <note>original: *Uredines*; a term borrowed from medicine and botany referring to a parching, destructive heat that consumes the "life" of the ore.</note> do when they overcome the metals. If the cold gains the upper hand, it brings the ore to ruin, degrading it even down to lead; indeed, it even drives it away entirely. But if the heat gains the upper hand, the metal becomes higher, nobler, and more alive the longer it lasts. This is the difference between heat and fire, or the powers of fire. ### Chapter 18 of the First Book.

A **foil** <note>original: *Folium*</note> is a **shedding** <note>original: *spolium*; refers to a skin or casing that is cast off, like that of a snake.</note>, because it is constantly cast off even as it puts on and raises itself up during its ascent. Miners have almost the same way of speaking about their **lustrous ore** <term>Glanz</term> <note>A term for bright, metallic ores like galena.</note> and **deceptive ore** <term>Blende</term> <note>Sphalerite or similar minerals that "blind" or deceive the miner because they look metallic but were historically difficult to smelt.</note>. It is—to provide a parable—like a fire in the midst of its heat and flame: first there is the **shimmer**, then the **embers**, and the **ashes** <note>original: *Båsel*</note> are the **shedding** <note>original: *spolium*</note>. One might imagine that if they only possessed gold, they could manage all these things, but without this process, it cannot be done. Learn first to **foliate** <note>to apply the foil</note> and **spoliate** <note>to strip or shed the layer</note>; then you can set the metal upon it, but not otherwise. 

Such **shimmer** and **glimmer** are visible once they are set, but the **purification** <term>Låuterung</term> is not seen, much like the **vapors** <term>Witterung</term> <note>In mining, this refers to the "weather" or exhalations of the earth that indicate the presence of ore.</note>. Now, the closer such a glimmer is to the **extraction**, the more it enters into a descending ore and the more poisonous it becomes, until the poison is taken from it by fire and water. Then it joins again with the **seed**, for from the seed comes the shimmer, and from the shimmer comes the glimmer. 

There lies here a fine little art to **tincture** <term>tingiren</term> <note>To transform a metal's properties or color using an alchemical agent.</note> more highly through the shimmer, when one brings it into the glimmer. However, one realization always leads to another; and just as one sees and learns from a **deceptive ore** <note>original: *Blende*</note> and a **lustrous ore** <note>original: *Glanz*</note> that no **choke-damp** <note>original: *Schwaden*; dangerous, suffocating gases in a mine.</note> is present, so too one senses it in this glimmer and shimmer in its **mirrors** <term>speculis</term> and night-lights. To **prepare** <term>præpariren</term> such shimmer and glimmer so that it is quickly deposited and then released again is the greatest feat of all; for it deposits with the highest poison found under the earth, and thus it settles and must be "smelled in" <note>absorbed as a vapor</note>. As for what a great poison the **stillness of Mercury** <term>Mercurii</term> <note>Mercury in its inactive or "resting" state, often associated with hazardous cold or vapors.</note> is, especially under the earth...

Earths indicate the unhealthy diseases that follow from them. ### CHAPTER 19.

### Of Soot and Ash.

As for the **white soot** of metals, which is a most precious **silver-garment** if only one introduces it into the **mercuries** <note>The "mercuries" refer to the essential fluid or spiritual state of the metal, not necessarily common quicksilver.</note>, it is astonishing that the lowest **corruption of the bodies** <note>The decaying or breaking down of the raw material.</note> of metals produces the highest results, and from the highest, the lowest are formed again. Conversely, that which is most public, and which people think they know and can do, is often the worst and most uncertain—perhaps because they do not know the right way.

# The 1st Book's 19th Chapter.

Now, with the help of the <term>burning agents</term> <note>original Latin: *uredinum*. In alchemy, this refers to corrosive substances or "blasts" of fire used to break down materials.</note>, one must extract the soot from all the **mercuries** <note>The essential spirits or fluid principles of the metals.</note>. Tell me now: which "garment" and which metal yields this best? I must say it is that of **Saturn** <note>The alchemical name for Lead.</note>. For an "earth," when ignited, gives off a smoke; that is, a specific kind of smoke, for the thicker the smoke is, the sootier it is. However, as many books as I have read and as many **laborants** <note>Practical alchemists or laboratory workers.</note> as I have seen, they have not been able to achieve this. Yet you find it in **Saturn**, provided you first convert it into an "earth" <note>A metallic calx or powdered oxide created through heat.</note>. This is the entire foundation: what else would you ignite to turn into ash and soot? There you have both—or rather all three—within: soot, ash, and earth; and the fourth is the "coal" or the color.

But I must report here that common laborers believe that when one speaks of the **mercury of bodies** <note>original: *☿ corporum*</note>, it refers to **prepared metallic mercury** <note>original: *☿ metallum præparirt*</note>, or when speaking of the **salts of bodies** <note>original Latin: *Salibus corporum*</note>, they think it is a salt like our common table salt, and that it must be identical in every way. They think the same of the soot and ash, though there is a vast difference; for wood-ash or stone-ash is a much different thing than the ash and soot of metals in color and form, and much more so in their power and potency. Therefore, in such matters, one must look to the power and the Work itself; from this, the name arises. You cannot talk it into existence, nor argue it, nor work it in; even if you and all those who follow you worked on it for a hundred years, it is not called a "work," but an **After-Work** <note>The process of perfecting or refining what nature has already produced in the earth.</note>. This is also the nature of the ash: for when one works the earth—the metallic earth, I mean—just as nature intends in the Work, the soot flies to the top, and the color remains in the middle,

**Of the Sludge and Lye.**

F

...[just as a person knows how to] manage bread carefully, so nature also manages its waste carefully and brings it forth to the light of day, so that it may be put to good use. In this way, the metal is also recognized as being present in the earth by the sludge <term>Schlich</term> <note>original: *Schlich*; in mining, this refers to the fine, muddy residue or "slimes" left over after ore has been crushed and washed.</note> that nature casts out. This sludge is the rock that nature has sucked dry during its labor and which falls away when it is not filled with metal. Because it also carries a portion of the ore with it, it is rightly called *Schlich*, because it thus slips away <note>The author is making a play on words between the noun *Schlich* and the German verb *schleichen*, meaning "to sneak" or "to slip away."</note> from the work and goes off secretly. 

Wherever such sludge is found, pay close attention, for it breaks off from the material <note>original: *Zeug*; a general term for the "stuff" or substance of the metal.</note> and from the workshop in which the metals <note>original: *metalla*</note> work and perform their duties. Such sludge is a certain indication that metal is present there. It is useful for making all kinds of vessels as one might desire; however, I do not place much importance on the form of the vessel, but rather everything depends on the material itself. 

People take so much trouble to obtain the right material for bricks and cupels <term>Capellen</term> <note>Small, porous bowls used by assayers and alchemists to refine precious metals through a process called cupellation.</note>; they try to achieve this by using burnt bones and vine-ash, but it is all in vain. Instead, prepare this sludge for yourself and dry it well. People often try to prepare the clay with iron filings or shavings, but truly, much good material is spoiled by what is added to it. When you wish to cast something, first test the loam <note>original: *Leimen*; a mixture of clay and sand used for molds and furnace linings.</note> thoroughly, for I have often seen the furnaces melt before the material within them did. This material [the sludge], however, does not melt, but holds firm and is better than glass. Miners <note>original: *Bergleute*</note> hold it dear because of the metal it carries with it. But if I were able to obtain it everywhere for my work, I would [take] the metal that is within it...

# CHAPTER XXI.
## CONCERNING THE DROSS AND SLOUGH
## of the seed. <note>original: *DE SCORIA ET EXUVIO spermatis*; in the alchemical worldview, metals were thought to grow from a "seed" or "sperm," producing waste as they matured.</note>

->or<-

## Of Sinter and Exhalations. <note>original: *Sinter und Schwaden*; "Sinter" refers to mineral crusts or scale, while "Schwaden" refers to the dross or vapors released by metals.</note>

The very outermost and final waste of metals is sinter <term>Sinter</term> <note>original: *Sinter*; a crust of mineral deposits often found where water drips or in the cooling of metals.</note>, which is nevertheless very good and harmless. I mean, however, the sinter that the metals <note>original: *metalla*</note> discard themselves through their internal fires <term>Vredines</term> <note>original: *Vredines*; likely a reference to the internal corrosive heat or "blights" that push impurities out of the maturing ore.</note>; then there is the slough <note>original: *exuvium*</note> that the weathering <term>Beywitterung</term> <note>original: *Beywitterung*; the natural process by which minerals mature and react with the air and water within the earth</note> leaves behind, which looks like a sinter. This is a different kind of sinter, similar to that which the smiths and the smelters produce here in the forge; for besides the fact that they are always moving their bodies <note>original: *corpora*</note>, they also purify themselves. For although the lyes <term>Laugen</term> <note>original: *Laugen*; metallic waters or solutions that wash through the earth</note> wash down the minerals <note>original: *mineralia*</note> and colors, the metals nonetheless also purify themselves, as can be seen in the sinter that every metal leaves behind in the fire, which is nevertheless not the same as this natural one. In this sinter, one certainly sees that metal is present; for the sinter of the minerals produced by weathering is indeed tangible, recognizable, and visible, so that every mining expert <term>Berg-Verständiger</term> knows it. But the metallic sinter is also found among the slags <term>Schlacken</term>, though it is unrecognizable, which is why the slags are brittle; otherwise, one could forge them or cast them very densely, as some have occasionally attempted to do, but they were unable to remove this sinter. But beneath the earth, near the metals and also near the lyes, one sometimes finds it quite pure, and it is of all the colors that the metals or ores are, except...

...[to assume] that it is empty or barren; for firstly, it smears like a mountain-soap <term>BergSeiffen</term> <note>original: *BergSeiffen*; a greasy, clay-like mineral often used as a lubricant or for cleaning</note>, yet it is not one. However, this sinter is distinguished from schlich <term>Schlich</term> <note>original: *Schlich*; the fine, heavy mud or concentrate produced when ore is ground and washed</note> in that schlich always carries gold or silver metal with it, while this is a refined and skimmed earthy powder [purged] of all metal.

As for the exhalations <term>Schwaden</term> <note>original: *Schwaden*; known to miners as "damps," these are the heavy, often lethal vapors that accumulate in mine shafts</note>, this provides a very fine account of the separation of the seed and the labor of all bodies. For when the work ceases and it has no more food—neither for the minerals nor for the bodies—and the luster <term>Schimmer</term> has now completely retreated into the glimmer <term>Glimmer</term> <note>here, the "shimmer" represents the vital metallic spirit, while "glimmer" or mica represents the physical, brittle matrix</note>, and the luster wishes to depart from the seed, then they separate. Thus, the bond between the luster and the seed breaks. This is called the exhalation <term>Schwaden</term>, which is a very terrible poison; for it kills everything that lives, especially that which breathes.

### The 1st Book, Chapter 27

[...the] **rods** toward the place where an ore is located. This occurs because the lower **vapors** <note>original: *Witterung*; in this context, it refers to the subtle mineral emanations or "weather" of the earth that the dowser senses</note> of the ore are also present there and move against one another. The [sunbeam] takes these vapors and leads them back down with it; therefore, it also presses the metal on the rod downward, as if it wanted to bring it back into the main deposit. For these vapors represent the balancing and **union** <note>original: *copulation*</note> of atmospheric influences; for the [sun]beam must receive its material here on this earth in which it is to work. It does not bring rain directly onto the earth; rather, it transforms the **earth-smoke** which rises up into rain, snow, and frost, and brings it back to the earth, pouring it over it. It acts in the same way with the **earth-vapors** which are caused by the "weathering" or vapors of the inner metals. When they rise up, the beam makes them heavy again here above—yet only heavy enough so that they can enter the <term>☉</term> <note>The alchemical symbol for Gold, often associated with the Sun's influence</note> and assist it in its fruitful work. 

When the beam is engaged in such work and has completed it, then such a **metal-rain** (as I may call it) strikes the metal as well, weighing it down. It stirs the **spirit** <note>original: *Ferch*; an archaic term for the life-force, essential spirit, or "blood" of a substance</note> in its **fluid state** <note>original: *lubrico*; literally 'slippery' or 'smooth'</note>, which previously rested in its **volatile state** <note>original: *volatili*</note> during the union, and drives it downward. For the beam does not push; rather, it helps the volatile spirit so that it immediately awakens in the fluid state. Thus, it draws the rod down with it much more forcefully than is usually the case with a **striking-rod** <note>original: *Schlagruhten*; a traditional dowsing rod used to locate mineral veins</note> that does not touch the metal itself, but only the bare vapors that have not yet been refined by the [heavenly] influence. One might not unfairly call such vapors—

For the **vapor** <term>Dampff</term> is the arrow which the **air** <term>Lufft</term> shoots, and it is either a good or a poisoned ray. For the air itself cannot be poisoned, any more than the heart can suffer sickness <note>The author argues that air is a pure, fundamental element; it merely carries the "poison" like a messenger rather than being transformed into poison itself.</note>; it is only the pestilence or the evil vapor within it that brings the harm. Therefore, not everyone dies, but only those into whom this same evil vapor enters. For we must all live by the air; it is not, nor can it become, evil. Therefore, beware of the vapor, or that same projectile of the air, which does such harm within it; thank God for the air, for you must live by it. 

Those who attribute this same evil vapor to the **stars** <term>Gestirn</term> <note>In early modern science, the "stars" or celestial bodies were believed to govern the movement and quality of minerals and gases deep underground.</note> do not do so wrongly, for they also rule with their light and master such vapors, hindering one another with their paths, and reversing or changing the **weather-influences** <term>Witterungen</term> <note>While *Witterung* usually means weather, here it refers to the specific astrological "influence" or "effluvia" emanating from the planets.</note>. Thus, such vapors become more or less frequent, as happens during **eclipses** <note>original: *Eclipsibus*; Latin for eclipses.</note>. 

For when the weather-influences of the stars cannot govern the lower air, then such shameful and poisonous mists and vapors rise up or grow stronger. Likewise, when the mists and vapors of the "lower stars" <note>This likely refers to terrestrial or subterranean echoes of celestial forces.</note> are also obstructed by the fire- and **stone-deposits** <term>Stein-Sätze</term>, they also create such vapor beneath the earth. And especially this deposit, because it is airy, is very harmful; for it wanders about and causes great blockages where there should be openness.

# CHAPTER XXXI.
# CONCERNING THE METALLIC WHETSTONE <note>original: *De Cote Metallico*</note>,

## Concerning the Stone-Deposit.

<image-desc>Faint pencil sketches in the left margin include a triangle and some illegible cursive markings.</image-desc>

When the air <note>In this context, "air" refers to subterranean vapors or gases.</note> is formed entirely from a piece of pure earth, it eventually becomes a stone. However, there are many kinds of stones, just as there are many substances <term>corpora</term> in the earth—notwithstanding that it is all called "earth." The longer this material lies there, the harder and firmer it becomes. Such a stone can be removed by no other means than fire, which then attacks the earth and finally consumes it; for it is and becomes the structural foundation of the earth <term>Erdfesten</term>, just as the ribs and bones are the foundations of a fish or flesh. These, too, the dear God will finally remove with fire. For this reason, the ancients burned their bodies; for although the flesh soon rots in the earth, the bones remain longer, and their best dissolution <term>Verwesung</term> is fire, in which they become ashes, which is an "earth-ash."

Such a deposit harms the metal, for it does not allow the vital air <term>Witterung</term> <note>The author views metals as living things that require "breath" or atmospheric influence to grow; the "Stone-Deposit" acts as a suffocating barrier.</note> to reach it, without which it cannot be alive; instead, it must withdraw—that is, die off. For nothing can pass through it as it does through the earth, which is permeated by the vital vapors, just as the sun’s rays pass through with their effects. This "air" <note>The solidified vapor forming the stone.</note> is found just as one finds no fish without bones <note>original: *Grad* — an archaic term for fishbones.</note>, for it is the earth’s fortification. When it breaks out here at the surface, it yields good whetstones, grinding stones, or touchstones <note>Stones used to test the purity of gold and silver.</note>; it allows no water

In it, the vapor tends to remain; it cannot enter or penetrate. However, it contains within itself the accompanying fire, albeit dispersed <note>original: *dispersum*</note>. The Tower of Babel perished for this reason—not because of the elements, but because bricks do not withstand water. The Pyramids still stand because of their good materials, as do other firm buildings, as the ruins testify, which have fallen due to destruction and tearing down, or have collapsed through earthquakes; which finally lifts this deposit.
